extracted.intended_audience: journalists, election analysts, and news consumers interested in how a news organization calls races
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and operational criteria used by the Associated Press to decide when to declare winners on election night, including data sources, accuracy thresholds, and decision-making workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trailing candidate cannot catch the leader
rubrics_metrics.description: The thing we are looking to do is answer one question -- can the trailing candidates catch the leader? When we determined that data makes it clear the trailing candidate can't catch the leader, that's when we are able to declare a winner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The AP will only call a race when its analysis shows no plausible path for a trailing candidate to overcome the leader. If any path to victory remains, however small, the AP holds off on declaring a winner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive use of available data
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions are based on analysis of the vote count, the election survey (vote cast), registration statistics, and 'basically all the data available' with the vote count at the heart of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AP integrates multiple data streams rather than relying on a single indicator: official vote returns as they arrive, registration and voting pattern statistics, and survey data to form an overall judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vote Cast survey methodology (not traditional exit polls)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vote Cast is a survey of the electorate executed across all 50 states, aiming to talk to more than 120,000 voters in the week leading up to election day and up until polls close; it reaches voters where they are to ask how they would or did cast their ballots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike traditional exit polls (which interview voters as they leave polling places), Vote Cast samples voters in advance and on election day to account for high advance voting; AP uses this as a critical input both to call races and to understand voter motivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: High accuracy standard (aim for 100% accuracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: We aim for our standard 100% accuracy. If we are not certain that the trailing candidates can't catch the leader, we hold off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The threshold for making a call is extremely conservative: if there is any reasonable uncertainty or a possible flip, AP will delay calling to preserve accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-tiered decision process requiring agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: For each race: a race caller looks at the state closely, works with an analyst; if both agree, the decision goes to a decision editor who reviews the work. All three must agree before a call. For battleground or pivotal states senior editors (VP, Washington bureau chief, executive editor) join the conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls are made by consensus across distinct roles (caller, analyst, decision editor) with escalation to top editors for high-stakes races. The process is not strictly linear; many people on the team monitor and must be satisfied before declaring a winner.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-specific timing based on historical and current indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: It is very rare to call a race right after polls close; only in a small number of states is that possible because past election data, electoral history, registration statistics, advance vote statistics, and survey results all align to show a commanding win.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing of calls depends on the state context—historical patterns and the composition of votes (e.g., proportion of advance ballots) can allow immediate calls in a few places, but most states require waiting for actual returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for jurisdictional rules and runoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: AP expects to declare winners in about 4,800 elections this November, 'assuming none go to a runoff,' noting some states (e.g., Georgia, Louisiana) have runoffs that affect final outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Election-calling must account for state-specific rules (runoff triggers, multi-stage contests) which can change the timeline and certainty of outcomes; AP adjusts expectations and decisions accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robust staffing, data collection, and quality control
rubrics_metrics.description: AP's decision team comprises about 60 people (several full-time on elections) and the total effort across AP is around 5,000 people on election night working to collect votes, count and quality-check them, analyze, publish, and declare winners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-volume staffing and explicit quality checks are part of the standard—calls rest on processes for collection, verification, and cross-checking of incoming data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservative approach: hold off if race could flip
rubrics_metrics.description: If we think it's possible the race could flip, that the trailing candidates have a path to victory, small as it might be, as long as that path exists, we can't say who has won yet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AP favors avoiding premature calls; even small theoretical paths to victory require continued caution and delay in declaring winners.
